en: Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.1 (SN 47.1, PTS SN v 141) 1. Ambapālivagga Ambapālīsutta Thus have I heard. On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in Ambapālī’s grove. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” they replied. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, when a noble disciple possesses four things, he has transcended the realm of Māra, he has passed beyond the domain of the Evil One; he is one who has entered the stream, one who is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. What are the four? Here, bhikkhus, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally experienced by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. He possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—virtues that are untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. When a noble disciple possesses these four things, bhikkhus, he has transcended the realm of Māra, he has passed beyond the domain of the Evil One; he is one who has entered the stream, one who is no longer subject to rebirth in the lower worlds, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further said this: “He who possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha, And in the Dhamma, and in the Saṅgha as well, Who possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones— That person is called a stream-enterer, No longer bound to the nether world, Fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination.”
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in Ambapālī’s Grove.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [he said].
“Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:

“Bhikkhus, this is the one-way path for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna; that is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four?”
Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

This, monks, is the one-way path for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna; that is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The first [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.2 (SN 47.2, PTS SN v 142) 1. Ambapālivagga Satisutta – Mindfulness “Bhikkhus, develop mindfulness. When mindfulness is developed, what benefit does one see for the development of mindfulness? One who is mindful, bhikkhus, dwells with a guarded mind. One who dwells with a guarded mind experiences a pleasant abiding here and now, and he has no remorse at the time of death. With the abandoning of the five lower fetters, he is due to reappear spontaneously [in the Pure Abodes] and there attain final Nibbāna without ever returning from that world. This is the benefit one sees for the development of mindfulness.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in Ambapālī’s Grove.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu should dwell mindful and clearly comprehending.”
This is our instruction to you.
And how, monks, is a monk mindful?
Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings …pe… he dwells contemplating mind in mind …pe… he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
In this way, monks, a monk is mindful.
And how, monks, is a monk clearly comprehending?
Here, monks, a monk acts with clear comprehension when going forward and returning; he acts with clear comprehension when looking ahead and looking aside.
He acts with clear comprehension when bending and extending his limbs; he acts with clear comprehension in wearing his outer robe, inner robe, and bowl;
he acts with clear comprehension in eating, drinking, chewing, and tasting; he acts with clear comprehension in defecating and urinating;
he acts with clear comprehension in going, standing, sitting, sleeping, waking, speaking, and remaining silent.
"In this way, monks, a monk is one who acts with clear comprehension.
Monks, a monk should dwell mindful and clearly comprehending.
This is our instruction to you."
The Second.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.3 (SN 47.3, PTS SN v 142) 1.
Ambapālivagga (The Chapter on Ambapālī)
The Discourse to the Bhikkhus On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park.
Then a certain bhikkhu approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, that bhikkhu said this to the Blessed One:

“It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
“In this very way, some foolish people here entreat me, and when the Dhamma has been spoken, they think only of following after me.
“Venerable sir, let the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief! Let the Sugata teach me the Dhamma in brief!”
“Perhaps I might understand the meaning of what has been spoken by the Blessed One; perhaps I might become an heir to what has been spoken by the Blessed One.
“Therefore, bhikkhu, you should purify the very beginning of wholesome states.
And what is the beginning of wholesome states?”
“Virtue that is quite purified and a view that is straight.

When, bhikkhu, your virtue is quite purified and your view is straight, then, bhikkhu, based upon virtue and established upon virtue, you should develop the four foundations of mindfulness in three ways.
What four?”
Here, bhikkhu, dwell contemplating the body in the body internally—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
or dwell contemplating the body in the body externally—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
or dwell contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
Dwell contemplating feelings in feelings— internally, externally, or both internally and externally—
ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
Dwell contemplating the mind as the mind internally,
or the mind externally,
or the mind both internally and externally— ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
Dwell contemplating phenomena in internal phenomena,
or in external phenomena,
or in both internal and external phenomena— ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
“Since you, bhikkhu, relying on virtue and established in virtue,
will thus develop these four foundations of mindfulness in this threefold way, then for you, bhikkhu, whatever night or day comes,
only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline.”
Then that bhikkhu, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One,
and keeping him to his right, departed. Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute,
that bhikkhu in no long time attained that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having realized it for himself through direct knowledge in this very life, he entered and dwelt therein.
He understood: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
And that monk became one of the arahants.
The Third.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.4 (SN 47.4, PTS SN v 144) 1.
Ambapālivagga
The Sāla Discourse.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Kosalans at Sālā, a brahmin village.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus... [as before] ...and said this:
“Bhikkhus, those bhikkhus who are new, recently gone forth, having lately come to this Dhamma and Discipline—
those bhikkhus, I say, should be encouraged, settled, and established by you in the development of the four foundations of mindfulness. Which four?
Come, friends, dwell contemplating the body as body, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a serene mind, concentrated, with one-pointed mind, for the sake of knowing the body as it truly is;
dwell contemplating feelings as feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a serene mind, concentrated, with one-pointed mind, for the sake of knowing feelings as they truly are;
dwell contemplating the mind as mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with a serene mind, concentrated, with one-pointed mind, for the sake of knowing the mind as it truly is.
"Abide contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with minds clarified, concentrated, and one-pointed, for the sake of knowing phenomena as they truly are.
And those monks who are trainees (*sekha*), who have not yet attained their goal but abide aspiring for the unsurpassed security from bondage—
they too abide contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with minds clarified."
Concentrated with one-pointed mind, they dwell contemplating the body in the body for the sake of full understanding of the body;
they dwell contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with minds clarified, concentrated with one-pointed mind, for the sake of full understanding of feelings;
they dwell contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with minds clarified, concentrated with one-pointed mind, for the sake of full understanding of the mind.

They dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with minds clarified, concentrated, with one-pointed minds, for the sake of the full understanding of phenomena.
And those monks, bhikkhus, who are arahants— whose taints are destroyed, who have lived the holy life, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained their own goal,
whose fetters of existence are utterly exhausted, and who are liberated through right gnosis— they too dwell contemplating the body in the body.
They dwell ardent, clearly comprehending, with a mind unified, serene, concentrated, and one-pointed, dissociated from the body;
they dwell contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, with a mind unified, serene, concentrated, and one-pointed, dissociated from feelings;
they dwell contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, with a mind unified, serene, concentrated, and one-pointed, dissociated from the mind.
“They dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, unified, with minds clarified, concentrated, with one-pointed minds, detached from phenomena. Monks,
those monks who are new, recently gone forth, having only lately come to this Dhamma and Vinaya—
those monks, monks, you should encourage, settle, and establish them in the development of these four foundations of mindfulness.”
The Fourth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 47.5 (SN 47.5, PTS SN v 145) 1.
Ambapālivagga
The Discourse on the Heap of the Unwholesome.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
There, the Blessed One said this:
“Monks, one who says, ‘a mass of unwholesome states,’ would be speaking correctly if they were to speak of the five hindrances.
For this, monks, is an entire mass of unwholesome states, namely, the five hindrances.
Which five?
The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, and the hindrance of doubt.
“A heap of the unwholesome,” monks, speaking rightly, one would say of these five hindrances.
For this, monks, is an entirely unwholesome heap, namely, the five hindrances.
“‘A mass of the wholesome,’ monks, one speaking rightly would say of the four foundations of mindfulness.
For this, monks, is an entirely wholesome mass, namely, the four foundations of mindfulness. Which four?”
Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
[likewise] in relation to feelings …pe… in relation to the mind …pe…
He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
“One who speaks of a ‘mass of the wholesome,’ monks, would be speaking correctly if they spoke of these four foundations of mindfulness.
For this alone, monks, is a mass of the wholesome, namely, the four foundations of mindfulness.”
