Ambapālivagga
The Sakuṇagghi Sutta:
“In the past, monks, a hawk suddenly swooped down upon a quail and seized it.
Then, monks, as the quail was being carried off by the hawk, it lamented thus:”
“We are indeed unfortunate and of little merit, we who have wandered outside our own range, into the domain of another.
Had we been moving within our own range, in our ancestral domain, this hawk would not have been a match for us in battle.
“But what, lāpa, is your own range, your ancestral domain?”
‘This is what is called “the place for throwing clods where ploughing is done.
Then, monks, the hawk, overconfident in its own strength and not restraining its own strength, released the lapwing bird, saying:
‘Go away, lapwing; even having gone there, you will not escape from me.’
Then, monks, the quail bird went to a place where ploughing was being done, a spot where clods of earth were thrown; having climbed upon a large clod, he stood there calling out to the hawk:
“Come now, hawk! Come now, hawk!
Then, monks, that hawk, overconfident in her own strength and disregarding his own strength, folded both wings and suddenly swooped down upon the quail bird.
When the lapwing bird, monks, knew, "This hawk has come very close to me," it then retreated into the hollow of that very clod of earth.
Then, monks, the hawk struck its breast right there.
For such is the fate of one who wanders outside his own range, in another's domain.
Therefore, monks, do not wander in what is not your own range, the domain of others.
For those who wander in what is not their own range, the domain of others, Māra will find an opportunity; Māra will find a foothold.
And what, monks, is the monk’s non-range, the domain of others?
That is to say, the five strands of sensual pleasure. Which five?

Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust; [sounds cognizable by the ear... smells cognizable by the nose... tastes cognizable by the tongue... tangibles cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.]
Sounds cognizable by the ear ... [and so on] ...
odors cognizable by the nose ... [and so on] ...
tastes cognizable by the tongue ... [and so on] ...
Tangible objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire,
and provocative of lust— this, monks, is a non-range for a monk, the domain of others.
Wander, monks, in your own range, in your own ancestral domain.
“Bhikkhus, for those who move within their own range, their own ancestral domain, Māra will find no opportunity; Māra will find no foothold.
And what, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu’s range, his own ancestral domain?
That is to say:”
The four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four?
Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings …pe… mind in mind …pe… phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
“Bhikkhus, this is a bhikkhu’s own resort, his ancestral domain.
The sixth.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 47.7 (SN 47.7, PTS SN v 148)
1. Ambapālīvagga:
The Discourse on the Monkey “Bhikkhus, there are inaccessible and uneven regions in the Himalayas, the king of mountains, where neither monkeys nor humans roam.
“Monks, there are inaccessible and uneven regions of Himavat, the king of mountains, where monkeys indeed roam, but not humans.
There are also level and delightful tracts of land in Himavat, the king of mountains, where both monkeys and humans roam.
There, monks, hunters set down sticky resin on the monkey paths to afflict the monkeys.”
In that case, monks, those monkeys who are not foolish by nature and not greedy by nature, upon seeing that ointment, avoid it from afar.
But that monkey who is foolish by nature and greedy by nature, having approached that ointment, seizes it with his hand;
he becomes stuck there.
Thinking, "I will free my hand," he grasps with his second hand;
there he becomes entangled.
Thinking, "I will free both hands," he grasps with his foot.
Thus he becomes stuck there.
Thinking, "I will free both hands and the foot," he seizes it with his second foot;
thus he becomes stuck there.
Thinking, “I will free both my hands and my feet,” he seizes it with his snout;
thus he becomes entangled there.
For in this way, monks, that monkey, having been outwitted, lies down exhausted, fallen into misfortune and ruin, at the hunter’s disposal to do with as he pleases.
“Having pierced him, monks, the hunter releases him right there onto those burning wood embers and departs wherever he wishes.
So it is, monks, for one who wanders outside his own range, in another’s domain.
Therefore, monks, do not wander outside your own range, in another’s domain.”
“Bhikkhus, for those who wander in what is not their own domain, in the territory of others, Māra will find an opportunity; Māra will find a foothold.
And what, bhikkhus, is the bhikkhu’s non-domain, the territory of others?
That is to say:”
The five strands of sensual pleasure.
Which five?
Forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire, and provocative of lust.
Sounds cognizable by the ear … [and so on] … odors cognizable by the nose … [and so on] … tastes cognizable by the tongue … [and so on] …
“Tangible objects cognizable by the body that are desirable, lovely, agreeable, pleasing, connected with sensual desire,
and provocative of lust— this, monks, is a non-range for a monk, the domain of others.
Wander, monks, in your own range, in your ancestral domain.”
“Bhikkhus, for those who move within their own range, their own ancestral domain, Māra will find no opportunity; Māra will find no foothold.
And what, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu’s range, his own ancestral domain?
It is this:”
The four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four?
Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings...

[and so on] ...he dwells contemplating mind in mind... [and so on] ...he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
“This, bhikkhus, is the domain of a bhikkhu, his own ancestral territory.
The seventh.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 47.8 (SN 47.8, PTS SN v 149)
1. Ambapālivagga Sūdasutta “Bhikkhus,
suppose a foolish, incompetent, and unskilled cook were presented with various kinds of curries for a king or a king’s high minister.
[He prepares] with sour tips, bitter tips, pungent tips, sweet tips, with those that are chewy and those that are not, with those that are salty and those that are not.
Yet, monks, that foolish, incompetent, and unskilled cook does not grasp the sign from his master:
"This soup today is pleasing to my master," or "He reaches for this," or "He takes much of this," or "He speaks in praise of this."
"Today my husband’s soup has an excess of sourness that pleases me;
he brings more of what is sour, he takes more of what is sour, or he speaks in praise of what is sour. Today my [soup] has an excess of bitterness...
or an excess of pungency... or an excess of sweetness... or it is salty today... or it is not salty today."

‘Today my master’s soup was salty,’ or ‘Today my master’s soup was unsalted and he liked it,’ or ‘He brought more of the unsalted,’ or ‘He took a large portion of the unsalted,’ or ‘He spoke in praise of the unsalted.
In that case, monks, that foolish, incompetent, and unskilled cook does not receive clothing, nor does he receive wages, nor does he receive bonuses.
For what reason?
Because, monks, that foolish, incompetent, and unskilled cook does not grasp the characteristic of his own master.

In the same way, monks, here a certain foolish, incompetent, and unskilled bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
As he dwells contemplating the body in the body, his mind does not become concentrated and the defilements are not abandoned.
He does not grasp that sign.
He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... [and so on]...

He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind …pe… he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
While he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, his mind does not become concentrated and the defilements are not abandoned.
Thus he does not grasp that sign.
That foolish, incompetent, and unskilled bhikkhu, monks, is neither an attainer of pleasant dwellings in this very life, nor an attainer of mindfulness and clear comprehension.
For what reason?
For in this way, monks, that foolish, incompetent, and unskilled monk does not grasp the sign of his own mind.
Just as, monks, a wise, competent, and skilled cook might present a king or a king’s high minister with various kinds of soups:
those that are sour, bitter, pungent, sweet, solid, soft, salty, and unsalty.
“Monks, that wise, competent, and skilled cook grasps the signs from his master:
‘Today this curry of mine pleases my master; he reaches for it, he takes much of it, or he speaks in praise of it.
Today my master’s curry is sour at the top; he reaches for what is sour at the top; he [takes much of] what is sour at the top…’”
Or she takes much; or she speaks in praise of what is sour. "Today my husband’s soup was bitter for me...
today it was pungent for me... today it was sweet for me... today it was salty for me...
today it was unsalted for me... today my husband’s soup was salty for me... or today it was unsalted for me. Or she praises what is unsalted.
"He brings [the salt] forward, or he takes much of the salt-free [food], or he speaks in praise of the salt-free.
Monks, that wise, competent, and skilled cook gains clothing, gains wages, and gains extra offerings. Why is that?
For just as that wise, competent, and skilled cook, monks, learns the signs of his own master, even so, monks, here a certain wise, competent,
and skilled bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body— ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
As he dwells contemplating the body in the body, his mind becomes concentrated and his defilements are abandoned.
Thus he grasps that sign.
He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … pe … he dwells contemplating the mind in the mind … pe …
He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
As he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, his mind becomes concentrated and his defilements are abandoned.
He grasps that sign.
“Monks, that wise, competent, and skilled monk is one who attains pleasant dwellings in this very life and attains mindfulness and clear comprehension.
For what reason?
Because, monks, that wise, competent, and skilled monk has grasped the sign of his own mind.”
The Eighth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.9 (SN 47.9, PTS SN v 152) 1.
Ambapālivagga (The Chapter on Ambapālī)
The Discourse on the Sick.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the village of Beluva.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Come, bhikkhus, spend the rains retreat each according to your friends, according to those you have seen, and according to those with whom you have shared meals, throughout the vicinity of Vesālī.
As for me, I shall enter the rains retreat right here at Veḷuva Village.”
“Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One, and they entered upon the rains retreat around Vesālī, each with their own friends, acquaintances, and associates.
But the Blessed One entered upon the rains retreat right there at the village of Veḷuva.
Then, while the Blessed One had entered upon the rains retreat, a severe illness arose in him; sharp, deathly pains assailed him.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, mindful and clearly comprehending, endured it without being disturbed.
Then this occurred to the Blessed One:
"It would not be fitting for me to attain final nibbāna without having addressed my attendants and without taking leave of the Saṅgha of bhikkhus."
"What if I were to dispel this illness through energy and dwell having resolved upon the life-faculty?
Then the Blessed One dispelled that illness through energy and dwelt having resolved upon the life-faculty.
Thereupon, the Blessed One's illness subsided.
Then the Blessed One, having recovered from his illness, not long after rising from that sickness, went out from the dwelling and sat down on a seat prepared in the shade behind the dwelling.

Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"I have seen, Bhante, that the Blessed One is at ease."
"It is seen, Bhante, that the Blessed One is enduring;
it is seen, Bhante, that the Blessed One is maintaining himself.
However, Bhante, my body feels as if it has become numb, the directions are no longer clear to me, and even the teachings do not come to mind because of the Blessed One’s illness."
"Moreover, Bhante, I had some small measure of comfort, thinking:
'The Blessed One will not pass away into final nibbāna until he has said something concerning the community of monks.
"But what, Ānanda, does the community of monks expect from me now?"
"Ānanda, I have taught the Dhamma by making no distinction between inner and outer;
there is no 'teacher's fist' regarding the teachings of the Tathāgata.
Now, Ānanda, suppose someone were to think thus:"
‘I shall lead the community of monks,’ or ‘The community of monks is under my direction’— if he were to think thus, Ānanda, he would surely say something concerning the community of monks.
But it does not occur to the Tathāgata, Ānanda,
either ‘I shall lead the community of monks’ or ‘The community of monks is under my direction.’
What, Ānanda, could the Tathāgata possibly say concerning the Saṅgha of bhikkhus?
Now, Ānanda, I am old, aged, advanced in years, having reached the final stage of life;
my age has turned eighty.
"Just as, Ānanda, an old cart is kept going by means of lashings, even so, Ānanda,
it seems that the body of the Tathāgata is kept going by means of lashings.
At whatever time, Ānanda, the Tathāgata, through non-attention to all signs, [abides] with regard to certain feelings..."
Having attained and dwelling in the signless concentration of mind through cessation, Ānanda, at that time the body of the Tathāgata becomes more comfortable.
Therefore, Ānanda, dwell with yourselves as an island, with yourselves as a refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge.
And how, Ānanda, does a bhikkhu dwell with himself as an island, with himself as a refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
[likewise] in regard to feelings ... [and so on].

He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind... and he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
In this way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells with himself as an island, with himself as a refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge.
"Whoever, Ānanda, now or after my passing, shall dwell with themselves as an island, with themselves as a refuge, with no other refuge;
with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge— these, Ānanda,
among the bhikkhus who desire training, will be the foremost."
The Ninth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.10 (SN 47.10, PTS SN v 154) 1.
Ambapālivagga
The Discourse on the Nuns’ Quarters.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Ānanda dressed, took his bowl and robe, and approached a certain nuns’ quarters. Having arrived, he sat down on the prepared seat.
Then a number of bhikkhunīs approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, [they paid homage to] the Venerable...
Having paid homage to Ānanda, they sat down to one side. Sitting there, those bhikkhunīs said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Here, venerable Ānanda, many bhikkhunīs, dwelling with their minds well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, perceive a sublime distinction between what was before and what is after.
"So it is, sisters; so it is, sisters."
“Sisters, for any bhikkhu or bhikkhunī who dwells with a mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness,
it is to be expected that they will perceive a sublime distinction between what was before and what comes after.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened those bhikkhunīs with a discourse on the Dhamma, rose from his seat and departed.
Then, after walking for alms in Sāvatthī, the Venerable Ānanda returned from his almsround after his meal and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, having dressed in the morning and taking my bowl and robe, I went to a certain nunnery; having arrived, I sat down on the prepared seat.
Then, Bhante, a number of bhikkhunīs approached me; having approached and paid homage to me, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, Bhante, those bhikkhunīs said this to me:”

“Here, Bhante Ānanda, a number of bhikkhunīs, dwelling with their minds well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, perceive a sublime distinction between what was before and what is after.
When this was said, Bhante, I said to those bhikkhunīs:
“So it is, sisters; so it is, sisters.”

“Sisters, for any bhikkhu or bhikkhunī who dwells with a mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, it is to be expected that they will perceive a sublime distinction between what was before and what comes after.
“So it is, Ānanda! So it is, Ānanda!

For any bhikkhu or bhikkhunī, Ānanda, who dwells with a mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness, it is to be expected that they will perceive a sublime distinction between what was before and what comes after.”
‘He will perceive a sublime distinction between what was before and what is after.
In which four?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
As he dwells contemplating the body in the body, there arises in him a fever of the body with the body as its object, or mental sluggishness, or his mind wanders externally.
Therefore, Ānanda, that bhikkhu should fix his mind upon some inspiring sign.
As he fixes his mind upon some inspiring sign, gladness is born in him.
In one who is joyful, rapture arises.
For one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil.
With a tranquil body, one experiences happiness.
The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.
He reflects thus:
"That purpose for which I directed my mind has been accomplished by me."
‘Now, indeed, I shall withdraw it.
He withdraws it, and neither thinks nor examines.
He understands: ‘I am without thought and without examination; mindful within, I am happy.’

Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … mind in mind … phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
As he dwells contemplating phenomena among phenomena, there arises in him a fever of the body with respect to those phenomena as its object, or mental sluggishness, or his mind wanders externally.
Therefore, Ānanda, that bhikkhu should direct his mind toward some inspiring sign.
As he directs his mind toward some inspiring sign, gladness is born in him.
In one who is joyful, rapture arises.
For one whose mind is rapturous, the body becomes tranquil.
With a tranquil body, one experiences happiness.
The mind of one who is happy becomes concentrated.
He reflects thus:
"That purpose for which I directed my mind has been accomplished by me."
‘Now, indeed, I shall withdraw it.
He withdraws it, and neither applies nor sustains thought.
He understands: ‘I am without applied thought and without sustained thought; mindful within, I am happy.’
In this way, Ānanda, there is development with a fixed intention.
And how, Ānanda, is there development without a fixed intention?
Having directed his mind away from the external, a bhikkhu understands: "My mind is not fixed on the external. This is development without a fixed intention.
Then he understands: "It is unconfined, liberated, and wishless both behind and before.
And yet he understands: "I dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful;
I am at ease. Having directed his mind externally, Ānanda, a bhikkhu understands: "My mind is wishless regarding the external."
Then he understands: "It is unconfined, liberated, and wishless both behind and before.
And yet he understands: "I dwell contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful;
I am happy. Having directed his mind externally, Ānanda, the bhikkhu understands: "My mind is wishless regarding the external."
Then he understands: "It is unconfined, liberated, and wishless both behind and before.
And yet he understands: "I dwell contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful;
I am at ease. Having directed his mind externally, Ānanda, a bhikkhu understands: "My mind is wishless regarding the external."
Then, afterwards, he understands: "It is uncontracted, liberated, and wishless.
And yet, he understands: "I dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful; I am happy.
In this way, Ānanda, there is development without directed intention.
"Thus, Ānanda, I have taught development with a specific aspiration, and I have taught development without a specific aspiration.
Whatever, Ānanda, should be done by a Teacher who seeks the welfare of his disciples and has compassion for them, out of compassion—that I have done for you.
Here, Ānanda, are the roots of trees; here are empty huts. Meditate, Ānanda; do not be negligent. Do not later fall into regret. This is my instruction to you."
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Ānanda, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Tenth.
The first chapter, the Ambapālī-vagga.
Its summary verse:
Ambapālī, the mindful bhikkhu.
The hall, the heap of wholesome states,
the hawk, the monkey, the cook,
the sick man, and the nuns’ quarters.

Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.11 (SN 47.11, PTS SN v 158) 2. Nālandavagga Mahāpurisa Sutta Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Nālandā in the Pāvārika Mango Grove. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, there are these four marks of a great man. Possessing which, a great man, a great person, is called a ‘great man. What four? (1) Here, bhikkhus, a great man has a well-proportioned body, neither too tall nor too short, neither too stout nor too thin, neither too dark nor too fair, but of moderate height and proportion. This is the first mark of a great man. (2) Again, a great man has a broad-shouldered body, with rounded shoulders, like a well-bred horse or a well-bred bull. This is the second mark of a great man. (3) Again, a great man has a straight body; his body is as straight as that of a well-bred horse or a well-bred bull. This is the third mark of a great man. (4) Again, a great man has a body that is well-knit and compact, like a well-bred horse or a well-bred bull. This is the fourth mark of a great man. Possessing these four marks of a great man, a great man, a great person, is called a ‘great man. When this was said, a certain bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Possessing these four marks of a great man, a great man, a great person, is called a “great man. But, venerable sir, how is it when a great man, a great person, does not become a world-ruling monarch? “It is, bhikkhu, because he does not fulfill the five powers. What five? (1) Here, bhikkhu, a great man possesses the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. It is because he does not fulfill these five powers that a great man, a great person, does not become a world-ruling monarch. But if he fulfills these five powers, then he becomes a world-ruling monarch. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘If he fulfills these five powers, then he becomes a world-ruling monarch. But, venerable sir, how is it when a great man, a great person, does not become a world-ruling monarch, but instead goes forth from the household life into homelessness? “It is, bhikkhu, because he does not fulfill the seven factors of enlightenment. What seven? (1) Here, bhikkhu, a great man possesses the factor of enlightenment that is mindfulness, which is supported by seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in relinquishment. (2) He possesses the factor of enlightenment that is investigation of states... (3) ...the factor of enlightenment that is energy... (4) ...the factor of enlightenment that is rapture... (5) ...the factor of enlightenment that is tranquility... (6) ...the factor of enlightenment that is concentration... (7) ...the factor of enlightenment that is equanimity, which is supported by seclusion, dispassion, and cessation, maturing in relinquishment. It is because he does not fulfill these seven factors of enlightenment that a great man, a great person, does not become a world-ruling monarch, but instead goes forth from the household life into homelessness. But if he fulfills these seven factors of enlightenment, then he becomes an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. When this was said, that bhikkhu said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘If he fulfills these seven factors of enlightenment, then he becomes an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. “Indeed, bhikkhu, it is so. It is so, bhikkhu. If a great man, a great person, fulfills these seven factors of enlightenment, then he becomes an arahant, one whose taints are destroyed. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, that bhikkhu delighted in the Blessed One’s words. *End of Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.11: Mahāpurisa Sutta.*
The setting was at Sāvatthī.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:
"Venerable sir, it is said: ‘A great person, a great person.’"
“To what extent, venerable sir, is one a great person?
“Sāriputta, it is because of the liberation of the mind that I say one is a ‘great person.
Because of the non-liberation of the mind, I say one is ‘not a great person.’”
And how, Sāriputta, is one liberated in mind?
Here, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
As he dwells contemplating the body as the body, his mind becomes dispassionate and is liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings … mind in mind … phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
As he dwells contemplating phenomena among phenomena, his mind becomes dispassionate and is liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
In this way, Sāriputta, one is one whose mind is liberated.
Because his mind is liberated, Sāriputta, I call him a "great person."
"Because his mind is not liberated, I say he is 'not a Great Man.
First.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 47.12 (SN 47.12, PTS SN v 159)
2. The Chapter on Nālandā:
The Discourse at Nālandā.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Nālandā in the Pāvārika Mango Grove.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Sitting to one side, the Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:

"I have such confidence in the Blessed One, Bhante, that there has never been, will never be, nor is there now, another ascetic or brahmin who is more distinguished than the Blessed One with regard to supreme enlightenment."
“Magnificent indeed is this bull-like speech uttered by you, Sāriputta; you have taken a definitive stand and let out a lion’s roar:

‘I have such confidence in the Blessed One, Bhante, that there has never been, will never be, nor is there now another ascetic or brahmin who is more distinguished than the Blessed One in regard to supreme enlightenment.’”
"Sāriputta, have you encompassed with your mind the minds of all those who were the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the past,

such that you have known of them: 'Those Blessed Ones had such virtue,' or 'Those Blessed Ones had such qualities,' or 'Those Blessed Ones had such wisdom,' or 'Those Blessed Ones dwelt in such a way'?"
“Or, ‘Those Blessed Ones were liberated in such a way’?”—
“Certainly not, Bhante.”— “But then, Sāriputta,
have you encompassed with your own mind the minds of all those who will be in the future time, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas, and known them thus:”
"Will those Blessed Ones have such virtue? or "Will those Blessed Ones have such qualities?
or "Will those Blessed Ones have such wisdom? or "Will those Blessed Ones abide in such a way?
or "Will those Blessed Ones be thus liberated?"
“No, venerable sir.
“But, Sāriputta, have you now, having encompassed my mind with your own mind, known me thus:

‘The Blessed One is of such virtue,’ or ‘The Blessed One is of such Dhamma,’ or ‘The Blessed One is of such wisdom,’ or ‘The Blessed One dwells in such a way,’ or ‘The Blessed One is liberated in such a way’?”
“No, venerable sir.
“In that case, Sāriputta, you do not possess the knowledge of encompassing the minds of the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, of the past, future, and present.
Then why, Sāriputta, have you uttered this sublime, bull-like speech, taken up a one-sided position, and roared this lion’s roar?”
“I have such confidence in the Blessed One, Bhante, that there has not been, will not be,
and is not now found any other ascetic or brahmin who is more distinguished than the Blessed One in regard to this supreme enlightenment.
“Bhante, I do not possess the knowledge of others' minds regarding the arahants, the perfectly enlightened ones, of the past, future, and present.”
Moreover, the sequence of the Dhamma is known to me.
Just as if, venerable sir, there were a king’s frontier city with strong ramparts, strong walls and arches, and a single gate;
and there was a gatekeeper there who was wise, competent, and intelligent, who kept out those he did not know and let in those he knew.
As he proceeds along the circumambulatory path all around that city, he would not see a joint in the wall or an opening in the wall, even one large enough for a cat to pass through.
He would think to himself:
"Whatever gross beings enter or exit this city, they all enter or exit through this very gate."
In the same way, Bhante, I have understood the underlying principle:
"Those who were the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, in the past— all those Blessed Ones,
having abandoned the five hindrances, which are mental defilements that weaken wisdom, [abided] in the four foundations of mindfulness..."
With well-established minds, having developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are, they fully awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
And those, Bhante, who will be Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones in the future time—
all those Blessed Ones, having abandoned the five hindrances— those defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom— in the four foundations of mindfulness...
With well-established minds, having developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are, they will awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
And now, venerable sir, the Blessed One is an arahant, a perfectly enlightened one, who has abandoned the five hindrances, those defilements of the mind.
“By weakening wisdom, with a mind well-established in the four foundations of mindfulness,
and having developed the seven factors of enlightenment as they really are, he has awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
“Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta!”
"Therefore, Sāriputta, you should frequently recite this discourse on the Dhamma to the bhikkhus, bhikkhunīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.

For those foolish men, Sāriputta, who may have doubt or uncertainty regarding the Tathāgata, their doubt or uncertainty regarding the Tathāgata will be abandoned upon hearing this discourse on the Dhamma.
This is the second [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.13 (SN 47.13, PTS SN v 161) 2. Nālandavagga Cunda Sutta At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Nāḷandā in Pāvārika’s Mango Grove. Then the householder Cunda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the householder Cunda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Cunda, there are these five aggregates subject to clinging. What five? The form aggregate subject to clinging, the feeling aggregate subject to clinging, the perception aggregate subject to clinging, the volitional formations aggregate subject to clinging, and the consciousness aggregate subject to clinging. These, Cunda, are the five aggregates subject to clinging. Whoever, Cunda, has developed and cultivated the four bases for psychic power, made them a vehicle, made them a basis, established them, maintained them, and mastered them, could, if he so wished, remain for the lifespan or for what is left of the lifespan. The Tathāgata, Cunda, has developed and cultivated the four bases for psychic power... and mastered them. If the Tathāgata so wished, he could remain for the lifespan or for what is left of the lifespan. When this was said, the householder Cunda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is amazing, venerable sir! How well the Blessed One has stated this: ‘The Tathāgata, Cunda, has developed and cultivated the four bases for psychic power... and mastered them. If the Tathāgata so wished, he could remain for the lifespan or for what is left of the lifespan. But, venerable sir, how is it that the Tathāgata does not exercise this mastery? “Cunda, the Tathāgata has abandoned the basis for attachment to existence, cut it off at the root, made it like a palm stump, done away with it so that it is no longer subject to future arising. Therefore, the Tathāgata does not exercise this mastery. Then the householder Cunda rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after the householder Cunda had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, let us go to Pāṭaligāma. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied. Then the Blessed One set out for Pāṭaligāma with a large community of bhikkhus. Now at that time, the Magadhan king Ajātasattu Vedehiputta had a new town built at Pāṭaligāma as a fortress. He had heard: “The ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from a Sakyan clan, is wandering among the Magadhans with a large community of bhikkhus, and he has arrived at Pāṭaligāma. Regarding that Blessed Gotama, a good report has been spread about: ‘That Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Enlightened One, the Blessed One. He declares this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and people, after realizing it through direct knowledge. He teaches a Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he reveals a holy life that is utterly perfect and pure. It is good to see such arahants. Then King Ajātasattu ordered the chief minister: “Go, master, and find out why this great crowd of people is gathered at Pāṭaligāma. “Yes, sire,” the chief minister replied, and he went to Pāṭaligāma. There he saw the great crowd of people gathered at Pāṭaligāma and asked them: “Why is this great crowd of people gathered here? “The ascetic Gotama, the son of the Sakyans who went forth from a Sakyan clan, is wandering among the Magadhans with a large community of bhikkhus, and he has arrived at Pāṭaligāma. Regarding that Blessed Gotama, a good report has been spread about... It is good to see such arahants. Then the chief minister returned to Rājagaha and reported this to King Ajātasattu. King Ajātasattu said: “Master, wherever the ascetic Gotama stays, that is where I shall stay. Then the chief minister went to the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: “Venerable sir, King Ajātasattu pays homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet and asks: ‘Where, venerable sir, will the Blessed One spend the rains retreat? “I shall spend the rains retreat right here in Pāṭaligāma, master. Then the chief minister thought: “This is wonderful, this is amazing! King Ajātasattu has said: ‘Master, wherever the ascetic Gotama stays, that is where I shall stay,’ and now the Blessed One says: ‘I shall spend the rains retreat right here in Pāṭaligāma. Let me then have the town fortified at Pāṭaligāma. Then the chief minister had the town at Pāṭaligāma fortified. He had watchtowers built at intervals of one league along the highway from Rājagaha to Pāṭaligāma, and he provided food supplies, fodder, and fuel at intervals of half a league. Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Pāṭaligāma as long as he liked, set out for Rājagaha with a large community of bhikkhus. After traveling by stages, he arrived at Rājagaha. There the Blessed One stayed at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground.

Then the householder Cunda, having heard that the Blessed One had arrived at Rājagaha and was staying in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Ground, approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the householder Cunda said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would accept tomorrow’s meal from me together with the community of bhikkhus. The Blessed One consented by silence. Then the householder Cunda, understanding the Blessed One’s consent, rose from his seat, paid homage to him, and keeping him on his right, departed. When the night had passed, the householder Cunda had excellent food, both hard and soft, prepared at his residence. He then had the time announced to the Blessed One: “It is time, venerable sir, the meal is ready. Then, it being morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and went with the community of bhikkhus to the residence of the householder Cunda. On arrival, he sat down on the appointed seat. Then the householder Cunda personally served the community of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha with the excellent food, both hard and soft. When the Blessed One had finished eating and had withdrawn his hand from the bowl, the householder Cunda took a low seat, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, there are these people who eat the leftovers from the meal of the householder Cunda. They say: ‘The householder Cunda is a fool, he is a sinner; he has eaten the meal of a poison-eater, he has eaten the meal of a killer. Venerable sir, how should we answer them? “Cunda, whoever says: ‘The householder Cunda is a fool, he is a sinner; he has eaten the meal of a poison-eater, he has eaten the meal of a killer,’ should be told: ‘Friend, the Blessed One did not die of that meal; the Tathāgata digested it properly. And you should also say: ‘Friend, when the Blessed One ate the truffle from the pot, that was the last food he consumed in this life. But because of that meal, the Blessed One suffered a severe illness accompanied by vomiting and bloody diarrhea. Yet even then, the Blessed One endured it mindfully and fully aware, without giving way to distress. Then the Blessed One addressed the Venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, let us go to the Gijjhakūṭa mountain. “Yes, venerable sir,” the Venerable Ānanda replied. Then the Blessed One went with a large community of bhikkhus to the Gijjhakūṭa mountain. On arrival, he said to the Venerable Ānanda: “
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Venerable Sāriputta was dwelling among the Magadhans at Nālakagāma, afflicted, suffering, and gravely ill.
And the novice Cunda was the Venerable Sāriputta’s attendant.
Then the Venerable Sāriputta attained final Nibbāna by means of that very illness.
Then the novice Cunda, taking the Venerable Sāriputta’s bowl and robe, went to Sāvatthī, to Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery, and approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he...
Having paid homage to Ānanda, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the novice Cunda said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
"Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna.
This is his bowl and robe."
“Friend Cunda, this is a subject that merits being brought before the Blessed One for his inspection.
Come, friend Cunda, let us approach the Blessed One; having approached him, we shall report this matter to the Blessed One.
“Very well, venerable sir,” the novice Cunda replied to the Venerable Ānanda.
Then the Venerable Ānanda and the novice monk Cunda approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, this novice Cunda says:
‘Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta has attained final nibbāna;
here is his bowl and robe.’”

"Moreover, Bhante, my body feels as if it has become numb; the directions are no longer clear to me, and even the teachings do not come to mind now that I have heard, 'The Venerable Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna.

"But what was it, Ānanda, that Sāriputta took with him when he attained final Nibbāna? Was it the aggregate of virtue, or the aggregate of concentration, or the aggregate of wisdom, or the aggregate of liberation?"
“Has he attained final Nibbāna, or has he attained final Nibbāna having taken up the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation?
“Venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta has not attained final Nibbāna having taken up the aggregate of virtuous behavior, nor the aggregate of concentration,
nor the aggregate of wisdom...”
...having taken up the aggregate of liberation ...pe...
or the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation, he has attained final Nibbāna.

Moreover, venerable sir, the Venerable Sāriputta was my instructor, one who had plunged into the depths, who made things understood, who showed the way, who incited, who inspired, and who gladdened; he was untiring in teaching the Dhamma and a helper to his fellow celibates.
“We remember that nourishment of the Dhamma, that wealth of the Dhamma, that support of the Dhamma from the Venerable Sāriputta.
“Was it not already declared by me, Ānanda, as a precaution:
‘There is separation, dissociation, and change regarding all things that are dear and pleasing’?”
How could it be possible here, Ānanda, that what is born, become, conditioned, and subject to disintegration should not disintegrate?
Such a thing is impossible.
Just as, Ānanda, from a large tree standing possessed of heartwood, its largest trunk might break off;
In the same way, Ānanda, Sāriputta has attained final Nibbāna while a great community of bhikkhus, possessed of essence, remains.
How could it be possible here, Ānanda? That what is born, become, conditioned, and subject to disintegration should not disintegrate—that is impossible.
Therefore, Ānanda, dwell with yourselves as an island, with yourselves as a refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge.
And how, Ānanda, does a bhikkhu dwell with himself as an island, with himself as a refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge?
Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings …pe… he dwells contemplating mind in mind …pe… he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
In this way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells as an island unto himself, with himself as his refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as his island, with the Dhamma as his refuge, with no other refuge.
For whoever, Ānanda, whether now or after I am gone, shall dwell as an island unto themselves, with themselves as their refuge, with no other refuge;
with the Dhamma as their island, with the Dhamma as their refuge, with no other refuge—it is these, Ānanda, who will be the foremost among my bhikkhus.
“Whoever desires to train. The third [discourse].
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 47.14 (SN 47.14, PTS SN v 163)
2. The Chapter on Nālandā:

The Discourse at Ukkacelā At one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Vajjis at Ukkacelā on the bank of the river Gaṅgā, together with a large Saṅgha of bhikkhus, not long after Sāriputta and Moggallāna had attained final Nibbāna.
Now at that time, the Blessed One was seated in the open air surrounded by the community of monks.
Then the Blessed One, having surveyed the silent community of monks, addressed the monks:
"Monks, this assembly appears as if empty to me now that Sāriputta and Moggallāna have attained final Nibbāna."
“Bhikkhus, my assembly is not empty; it is not neglected in that direction where Sāriputta and Moggallāna dwell.

For whatever Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones there were in the past, even for those Blessed Ones, such was the maximum extent of their pair of chief disciples—just as Sāriputta and Moggallāna are mine.”

“Bhikkhus, whatever Arahants, Perfectly Enlightened Ones there may be in the future, for those Blessed Ones too there will be a pair of chief disciples no greater than this—one such as Sāriputta and Moggallāna are for me.
It is wonderful, bhikkhus, regarding these disciples; it is marvelous, bhikkhus, regarding these disciples!
They will indeed carry out the Teacher’s instruction, they will act upon his advice, and they will be dear and pleasing to the four assemblies, as well as respected and esteemed.”
“It is wonderful, monks, for the Tathāgata; it is marvelous, monks, for the Tathāgata.
Even when such a pair of disciples has attained final Nibbāna, there is no sorrow or lamentation in the Tathāgata.
For how could that be possible, monks? That what is born, become, conditioned, and subject to disintegration should not disintegrate—that is simply impossible.”
This is impossible.
Just as, monks, when a great tree stands possessed of heartwood, its largest trunks might decay;
even so, monks, while the great Saṅgha of bhikkhus stands possessed of heartwood, Sāriputta and Moggallāna have attained final Nibbāna.
How could this be possible, monks? That what is born, become, conditioned, and subject to disintegration should not disintegrate—that is simply not possible.
Therefore, monks, dwell with yourselves as an island, yourselves as a refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge.
And how, monks, does a monk dwell with himself as an island, with himself as a refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge?
Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
[likewise] in relation to feelings... [and so on].
He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind ... and phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
In this way, monks, a monk dwells with himself as an island, with himself as his refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as his refuge, with no other refuge.
“Bhikkhus, whoever now, or after my passing, shall dwell with themselves as an island, with themselves as a refuge and no other refuge;
with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge and no other refuge— these bhikkhus, bhikkhus,
will be foremost among those who desire training.”
The Fourth.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.15 (SN 47.15, PTS SN v 165) 2.
Nālandavagga
The Bāhiya Sutta.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.

Then the Venerable Bāhiya approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Bāhiya said this to the Blessed One:

“It would be well, venerable sir, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
“Therefore, Bāhiya, you must first purify the very beginning of wholesome states.
And what is the beginning of wholesome states?”
"Virtue that is quite purified and a view that is straight.
But when, Bāhiya, your virtue shall be quite purified and your view straight, then, Bāhiya, supported by virtue and established in virtue, you should develop the four foundations of mindfulness.
Which four?"

Here, Bāhiya, dwell contemplating the body as the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world; [dwell] contemplating feelings as feelings...
the mind as the mind... [and mental phenomena as mental phenomena].
Dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
Since you, Bāhiya, will thus develop these four foundations of mindfulness based on virtue and established in virtue,
then for you, Bāhiya, whether night or day comes, only growth is to be expected.
“...there is no falling away from wholesome states.
Then the Venerable Bāhiya, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Bāhiya—in no long time—[attained that goal] for the sake of which...
Those sons of noble family went forth from the home life into homelessness in the right way;
and having realized for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the supreme goal of the holy life, he dwelt therein.
He directly knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being."
And the venerable Bāhiya became one of the arahants.
Thus ends the fifth [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 47.16.
2. The Chapter on Nālanda;
The Discourse to Uttiya.
The setting was at Sāvatthī.
Then the Venerable Uttiya approached the Blessed One... [as before] ...and sitting to one side, the Venerable Uttiya said this to the Blessed One:
"It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute.
"Therefore, Uttiya, you should first purify the very beginning among wholesome states."
And what is the beginning of wholesome states?
It is virtue that is perfectly purified and a view that is straight.
Now, Uttiya, when your virtue is perfectly purified and your view is straight, then, Uttiya, relying on virtue and established in virtue, you should develop the four foundations of mindfulness.
Which four?

Here, Uttiya, dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world; [dwell] contemplating feelings in feelings... [and so on].
“Dwell contemplating the mind in the mind... and phenomena in phenomena—ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
Since you, Uttiya, will thus develop these four foundations of mindfulness based on virtue and established in virtue, you, Uttiya, will go beyond the realm of Death.”

Then the Venerable Uttiya, having rejoiced and delighted in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Then, dwelling alone, withdrawn,

diligent, ardent, and resolute, the Venerable Uttiya in no long time attained that supreme goal of the holy life for the sake of which sons of good family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness.
Having realized it for himself with direct knowledge in this very life, he entered and dwelt therein.
He directly knew: "Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.
And thus the Venerable Uttiya became one of the Arahants.
The Sixth.
Saṁyutta Nikāya 47.17 (SN 47.17, PTS SN v 166) 2.
Nālandavagga
The Noble Discourse:
“Bhikkhus, these four foundations of mindfulness, when developed and cultivated, are noble and emancipating; they lead the one who practices them to the complete destruction of suffering.
What are the four?”
Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
[likewise] in regard to feelings …pe… in regard to the mind …pe…
He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
These, monks, are the four foundations of mindfulness; when developed and cultivated, they are noble and emancipating, and lead the one who practices them to the complete destruction of suffering.
Thus ends the seventh [sutta].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.18 (SN 47.18, PTS SN v 167) 2. Nālandavagga Brahmasutta At Sāvatthī. Then the Brahmā Sahampati approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, stood to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach the Dhamma in brief. Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, the bhikkhus will dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Brahmā, there are these four establishments of mindfulness. What four? Here, Brahmā, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. These, Brahmā, are the four establishments of mindfulness. When this was said, the Brahmā Sahampati said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Dhamma been made clear by the Blessed One in many ways. I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dhamma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life shall last.”
At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Uruvelā on the bank of the river Nerañjarā at the Goatherd’s Banyan Tree, having recently attained full enlightenment.
Then, while the Blessed One was alone in seclusion, this reflection arose in his mind:

“This is the one-way path for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna; that is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness.”
Which four?
A bhikkhu might dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
or a bhikkhu [might dwell] contemplating feelings in feelings... [and so on].

Or a bhikkhu might dwell contemplating mind in the mind, or a bhikkhu might dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

This is the one-way path for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true way, and for the realization of Nibbāna; that is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness.”
Then Brahmā Sahampati, having understood with his own mind the reflection that had arisen in the Blessed One’s mind—
just as a strong man might extend his drawn-in arm or draw in his extended arm—
disappeared from the Brahma-world and reappeared before the Blessed One.
Then Brahmā Sahampati, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, extended his joined palms toward the Blessed One and said this to the Blessed One:
"So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata.
This, Bhante, is the one-way path for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the passing away of pain and dejection..."
For the sake of the destruction of ignorance, for the attainment of true knowledge, and for the realization of Nibbāna, namely: the four foundations of mindfulness.
What are the four?
Here, venerable sir, a bhikkhu might dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
Or, venerable sir, a bhikkhu might dwell contemplating feelings in feelings...
or, venerable sir, a bhikkhu might dwell contemplating mind in mind...
or, venerable sir, a bhikkhu might dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.

“Venerable sir, this is the one-way path for the purification of beings, for the surmounting of sorrow and lamentation, for the disappearance of pain and grief, for the attainment of the true method, and for the realization of Nibbāna; that is to say, the four foundations of mindfulness.
This is what Brahmā Sahampati said.
Having said this, he further spoke as follows:
“The one who sees the end of birth knows the single path,
the way that leads to welfare, out of compassion for the world.”
By this path those of old crossed over;
those who will cross and those who are crossing the flood do so by this same way.
Thus ends the eighth [verse].

Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.19 (SN 47.19, PTS SN v 168) 2. Nālandavagga Sedakasutta At Sāvatthī. “Monks, just as, when rain pours down in thick droplets on a mountain top, the water flows down following the slope; in the same way, monks, for a bhikkhu who dwells with a mind well-restrained by mindfulness, whatever evil, unwholesome states arise, they flow away following that mindfulness. “Just as, monks, when rain pours down in thick droplets on a mountain top, the water flows down following the slope and fills the clefts, gullies, and creeks; and when the clefts, gullies, and creeks are filled, they fill the pools; and when the pools are filled, they fill the lakes; and when the lakes are filled, they fill the rivers; and when the rivers are filled, they fill the great ocean—in the same way, monks, for a bhikkhu who dwells with a mind well-restrained by mindfulness, whatever wholesome qualities there are, they all converge in that mindfulness.”
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sumbhas at a town of the Sumbhas named Sedaka.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, once in the past, a bamboo-worker, having raised his bamboo pole, addressed his apprentice, Medakathālika, thus:”
"Come, friend Medakathālika, climb the bamboo pole and stand upon my shoulders.
"Yes, teacher," the pupil Medakathālika replied to the bamboo-pole man, and having climbed the bamboo pole, he stood upon the teacher's shoulders.
Then, monks, the bamboo-pole man said this to his pupil Medakathālika:
“‘Friend Medakathālika, protect me and I will protect you.
In this way, guarding one another and protecting one another, we shall display our skills, receive our rewards, and descend safely from the bamboo pole of the Caṇḍālas.
When this was said, monks, the pupil Medakathālika said this to the Caṇḍāla bamboo-pole performer:”
“But this will not be so, teacher.
Teacher, you protect yourself; I shall protect myself.
Thus, guarding ourselves and protecting ourselves, we will display our skills, receive our rewards, and descend safely from the bamboo pole.”
“Therefore, in this matter, there is a method,” the Blessed One said, “just as the pupil Medakathālika spoke to his teacher:
‘Monks, thinking “I will protect myself,” one should cultivate the foundations of mindfulness;
thinking “I will protect another,” one should cultivate the foundations of mindfulness.’”
“Bhikkhus, by protecting oneself, one protects others; by protecting others, one protects oneself.
And how, bhikkhus, does one protect oneself and thereby protect others?
By repeated practice, development, and cultivation.”
In this way, monks, by protecting oneself, one protects others.
And how, monks, by protecting others, does one protect oneself?
Through patience, non-violence, a mind of loving-kindness, and compassion.
In this way, monks, by protecting another, one protects oneself.
Thinking, "I shall protect myself," the establishment of mindfulness should be practiced;
thinking, "I shall protect another," the establishment of mindfulness should be practiced.
“Bhikkhus, by protecting oneself, one protects others; by protecting others, one protects oneself.
Thus was the ninth [discourse]. *Saṃyutta Nikāya* 47.20.
2. The Chapter on Nālandā:
The Discourse on the Most Beautiful Woman in the Land.
Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sumbhas at a town of the Sumbhas named Sedaka.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus!"
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, it is just as if a great crowd of people were to gather together, saying, ‘The beauty of the land! The beauty of the land!’”
“Furthermore, monks, that village beauty was supremely skilled in dancing and supremely skilled in singing;
thinking, ‘The village beauty dances and sings,’ a great crowd of people would gather even more than before.
Then a man might come who desires life, does not desire death, desires happiness, and is averse to suffering.”
One might say to him:
"Good man, you must carry this bowl of oil filled to the brim between the great public festival and the most beautiful woman of the land.
And a man with a raised sword shall follow closely behind you."
‘Wherever he might even slightly spill it, right there he would cause his head to fall.
What do you think, monks?
Would that man, disregarding that oil bowl, bring about negligence regarding anything external?”
“No, venerable sir.
“Monks, this simile has been given by me for the purpose of making the meaning known.
And this is the meaning here:”
“‘A bowl of oil filled to the brim,’ monks, is a designation for mindfulness directed to the body.
Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus:
‘Mindfulness directed to the body shall be developed by us, cultivated, made a vehicle, made a foundation, established, consolidated, and well undertaken.’”
“Thus indeed, monks, should you train yourselves.
The tenth [sutta].
The second chapter, the Nālandā Chapter.
Its summary verse:
Mahāpurisa, Nālandā,
Cunda, Cela, and Bāhiya.
The noble Brahmā Uttiya [spoke] concerning the country of Sedaka.
*Saṃyutta Nikāya* 47.21 (SN 47.21, PTS SN v 171).
3. Sīlaṭṭhitivagga Sīlasutta Thus have I heard:
On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda and the Venerable Bhadda were staying at Pāṭaliputta in the Kukkuṭa Monastery.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Bhadda emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Ānanda. Having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, the Venerable Bhadda said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“Friend Ānanda, regarding these wholesome virtues that have been spoken of by the Blessed One—what is the purpose for which these wholesome virtues were spoken of by the Blessed One?
“Excellent, excellent, friend Bhadda!
Your inquiry is indeed excellent, friend Bhadda; your ingenuity is excellent, your intuition is excellent; it is a noble and thorough question.”
“Is it not so, friend Bhadda, that you ask:
‘Friend Ānanda, regarding these wholesome virtues spoken of by the Blessed One—what is the purpose for which these wholesome virtues were spoken of by the Blessed One?
“It is so, friend,” he replied.

“Friend Bhadda, those wholesome virtues that have been spoken of by the Blessed One—these wholesome virtues have been spoken of by the Blessed One precisely for the sake of developing the four foundations of mindfulness. Which four?
Here, friend, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.”

He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings …pe… mind in mind …pe… phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
"Friend Bhadda, these wholesome virtues that have been spoken of by the Blessed One have been spoken of by the Blessed One precisely for the sake of developing these four foundations of mindfulness.
Thus it was said. First.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.22. (SN 47.22, PTS SN v 172)
3. Sīlaṭṭhitivagga Ciraṭṭhitisutta.
The same setting.
Sitting to one side, the Venerable Bhadda said this to the Venerable Ānanda:
“What, friend Ānanda, is the cause, what is the reason, why the true Dhamma does not endure for long after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna?
And what, friend Ānanda, is the cause, what is the reason, why the true Dhamma endures for long after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna?”
“Excellent, excellent, friend Bhadda!
Your penetration is indeed excellent, friend Bhadda; your ingenuity is excellent; your inquiry is admirable.
For it is thus that you ask, friend Bhadda:”
“Friend Ānanda, what is the cause, what is the reason why, after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the true Dhamma does not endure for long?
And what, friend Ānanda, is the cause, what is the reason why, after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the true Dhamma endures for long?

But, friends, it is because the four foundations of mindfulness have been developed and cultivated that, after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna, the true Dhamma endures for long. Which four? [The passage continues with the description of each foundation.]”
Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
[likewise] in regard to feelings … mind … [and likewise] … [mental phenomena].
He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
It is, friends, because these four foundations of mindfulness have not been developed and cultivated that the true Dhamma does not endure long after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna.
But it is, friends, because these four foundations of mindfulness have been developed and cultivated that the true Dhamma endures long after the Tathāgata has attained final Nibbāna.”
The Second.
Saṃyutta Nikāya 47.23 (SN 47.23, PTS SN v 173) 3. Sīlaṭṭhitivagga (The Chapter on the Stability of Virtue)
The Discourse on Decline.
On one occasion the Venerable Ānanda and the Venerable Bhadda were dwelling at Pāṭaliputta in the Kukkuṭa Monastery.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Bhadda emerged from seclusion and approached the Venerable Ānanda; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Venerable Ānanda.
Having exchanged greetings and pleasantries, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Bhadda said to the Venerable Ānanda:
"What, friend Ānanda, is the cause, what is the reason for the decline of the true Dhamma?
What, friend Ānanda, is the cause, what is the reason for the non-decline of the true Dhamma?"
“Excellent, excellent, friend Bhadda!
Your penetration is indeed excellent, friend Bhadda; your ingenuity is excellent, and your inquiry is admirable.
For it is thus that you ask, friend Bhadda:”
“Friend Ānanda, what is the cause, what is the reason for the decline of the true Dhamma?
And what, friend Ānanda, is the cause, what is the reason for the non-decline of the true Dhamma?
“It is so, friend,” [he replied].
“Friends, through the non-cultivation and non-multiplication of the four foundations of mindfulness, there is the decline of the true Dhamma.
And through the cultivation and multiplication of the four foundations of mindfulness, there is no decline of the true Dhamma. Which four?”
Here, friends, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body as a body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world;
[he dwells] contemplating feelings as feelings... the mind as mind... [and so on].
“He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
It is, friends, through the non-development and non-cultivation of these four foundations of mindfulness that there is the decline of the true Dhamma.
And it is, friends, through the development and cultivation of these four foundations of mindfulness that there is no decline of the true Dhamma.”
The Third.

The Discourse to a Certain Brahmin.
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then a certain brahmin approached the Blessed One; having approached, he exchanged greetings with the Blessed One.
When they had concluded their polite and courteous conversation, he sat down to one side. Sitting there, that brahmin said this to the Blessed One:

When this was said, that brahmin addressed the Blessed One:

Then the householder Mānadinna approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, how many things does a noble disciple possess that makes him worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world? “A noble disciple, householder, possesses four things that make him worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. What four? Here, householder, a noble disciple is possessed of virtue; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, consummate in his behavior and sphere of activity; he trains himself, having undertaken the training rules, seeing danger in the slightest faults. He is one who has learned much, who remembers what he has learned, and who accumulates the teachings he has learned; those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which proclaim the perfectly complete and pure spiritual life—such teachings he has learned much of, retained in mind, recited verbally, mentally investigated, and penetrated well by view. He possesses the noble eye of wisdom; he sees the noble Dhamma with that eye of wisdom, and he sees the Dhamma that is beyond death, which leads to the complete destruction of suffering. A noble disciple, householder, who possesses these four things is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world. When this was said, the householder Mānadinna said to the Blessed One: “Magnificent, venerable sir! Magnificent, venerable sir! Just as if one were to set upright what had been overturned, or to reveal what was hidden, or to show the way to one who was lost, or to bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, in the same way the Blessed One has explained the Dhamma in various ways. Then the householder Mānadinna, having delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words, rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Not long after the householder Mānadinna had left, the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a young corn-stalk, the person who is like a middle-aged man, the person who is like an old man, and the person who is like a tathāgata. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a young corn-stalk? Here, a certain person is virtuous, but he does not encourage others in virtue; he is himself learned, but he does not encourage others in learning; he is himself established in the noble eye of wisdom, but he does not encourage others in the noble eye of wisdom. This is called a person who is like a young corn-stalk. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a middle-aged man? Here, a certain person is virtuous and encourages others in virtue; he is himself learned and encourages others in learning; he is himself established in the noble eye of wisdom and encourages others in the noble eye of wisdom. Here, a certain person is not himself virtuous, nor does he encourage others in virtue; he is not himself learned, nor does he encourage others in learning; he is not himself established in the noble eye of wisdom, nor does he encourage others in the noble eye of wisdom. This is called a person who is like an old man. And how, bhikkhus, is a person like a tathāgata? Here, a certain person is himself virtuous and encourages others in virtue; he is himself learned and encourages others in learning; he is himself established in the noble eye of wisdom and encourages others in the noble eye of wisdom. This is called a person who is like a tathāgata. These, bhikkhus, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having said this, the Sublime One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, not long after the Blessed One had left, a certain bhikkhu approached the Venerable Ānanda and said to him:

Āsavasutta:
“Bhikkhus, there are these three taints.
Which three?”
The taint of sensual desire, the taint of existence, and the taint of ignorance—
these, monks, are the three taints.
For the abandoning of these three taints, monks, the four foundations of mindfulness should be developed.
Which four?

“He dwells contemplating the mind in the mind... and he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
Indeed, monks, these four foundations of mindfulness are to be developed for the abandoning of these three taints.”
The tenth.

The Deathless, its origin, and the path;

Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world; [he dwells] contemplating feelings in feelings... [and so on].

“Bhikkhus, there are these five higher fetters.”
Which five?
Lust for the form realm, lust for the formless realm, conceit, restlessness,
and ignorance— these, monks, are the five higher fetters.
